name: Composite facelift

lead: The composite facelift is a surgical facelift technique in which the skin, the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and the orbicularis oculi muscle around the eye are raised and repositioned together. It extends the lift into the midface and lower eyelid area, which standard lower-face lifts do not usually reach.
Published support consists mainly of surgeon-authored technique descriptions and case series. Comparative trials against other facelift methods were not found in the available literature.

paras: Dissection goes beneath the SMAS so that skin and deeper tissue move as a single flap. Proponents describe pairing an upward-and-outward pull on the lower face with an upward-and-inward pull on the cheek and lower eyelid region to balance the result.

As with other facelifts, documented complications include hematoma, nerve injury, scarring and skin necrosis, with smoking raising risk. Deeper planes bring dissection closer to facial nerve branches. It is performed by licensed surgeons under anesthesia.

lead: The composite facelift is a surgical rhytidectomy technique that elevates the skin, the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and the orbicularis oculi muscle together, extending into the periorbital region to address descent of the midface and the lower eyelid to cheek junction.[1][2] It is described as a modification of the deep-plane facelift.[1]

A 2008 surgical review describes the technique as a comprehensive approach that repositions essentially every deep structure of the aging face, including the neck, lower face, midface and lower eyelid junction, and forehead, balancing a superior-lateral vector in the lower face with a superior-medial vector in the cheek and lower eyelid.[3] The same source states that patients with stigmata of a previous facelift, such as a lateral sweep or hollow eyes, may be corrected with it.[3]

Published evidence consists mainly of surgeons' descriptions of their own technique and small series, including a report on esthetic outcomes after facial soft-tissue reconstruction using deep dissection and composite facelift technique.[4] No randomized trial comparing it with other facelift approaches was found. In looksmaxxing communities it falls under hardmaxxing, meaning surgical intervention.
infobox: Lower face, midface, lower eyelid junction[3]
Established surgical technique; evidence mostly case series

paras: Facial aging involves descent of the jowls, deepening of the nasolabial fold and changes to the lower eyelid, along with skin aging.[1] In the composite technique the surgeon raises skin, SMAS and orbicularis oculi as one composite flap, which is supplied by branches of the facial, angular and inferior orbital arteries, and which proponents say allows tightening with less reliance on skin tension.[1]

A classic French review of middle-third rejuvenation lists composite facelift alongside subcutaneous facelift, SMAS and platysma retightening, deep facelift and the facelift of the superficial adipo-cutaneous system as techniques designed to return migrated skin, fat and fibromuscular layers to a normal position, and notes that the middle third of the face is the most difficult region to correct.[2]

Deep-plane approaches work beneath the SMAS and release retaining ligaments that anchor skin to bone, notably the zygomatic and mandibular ligaments, so that the tissue becomes mobile.[1] Dissection is considered more technically demanding because it passes closer to facial nerve branches, although those branches supply muscle from their deep surface.[1]

A cadaver study of the anterior midcheek examined the Melo fat pad and its possible role in early recurrence of nasolabial fold laxity after facelift, and explored alternative surgical methods to prolong correction.[5] A small preliminary study using lymphoscintigraphy compared swelling clearance after different rhytidectomy techniques in three patients, challenging the assumption that deeper dissection always causes longer swelling.[6]

For facelifts in general, hematoma is the most common complication, followed by nerve injury (the greater auricular nerve being the most often injured sensory nerve and the facial nerve the most injured motor nerve), skin necrosis, scarring, hair loss at incisions, and ear distortion.[1] Smoking has been reported to raise the risk of skin necrosis roughly twelvefold.[1] Patients are typically asked to stop aspirin and blood thinners before surgery.[1]

Available human data are surgeon-reported. A 2008 article describes the extended SMAS and composite technique and its aims.[3] A 2013 oral and maxillofacial surgery paper reports esthetic outcomes after deep dissection and composite facelift technique used in facial soft-tissue reconstruction.[4] A 2026 paper describes a double-sling variant of the composite facelift.[7] A registered trial (NCT04543318) concerns nerve transfer for eyelid paresis rather than the cosmetic facelift itself.[8] No randomized comparisons of composite facelift against other facelift types were found.

timeline.event: The SMAS is described anatomically, enabling later deep-layer facelifts.[1]
Composite facelift is listed among techniques for middle-third rejuvenation in a French review.[2]
Surgical review describes extended SMAS dissection and composite rhytidectomy.[3]
A double-sling composite facelift variant is published.[7]
